title: Insurable Home in California: FAIR Plan Spreads to Low-Risk ZIPs
subtitle: In 396 ZIP codes, the insurer of last resort is now writing mostly homes its own model calls low-risk. Geography alone no longer answers the coverage question.

our_perspective: When the ZIP code stops explaining who gets covered, the building has to make its own case. That is a design brief, not a paperwork exercise. California's Safer from Wildfires program lists twelve mitigation measures, and insurers must offer a discount for each one adopted; we treat those twelve as drawing-board inputs rather than a retrofit checklist. Enclosed eaves, non-combustible soffits, WUI-compliant vents, a non-combustible Zone 0 perimeter, an envelope of ICF reinforced concrete: in our villas these are resolved inside the architecture itself, the way the Italian villa has always folded climate into its form. A home that can be read clearly by an underwriter is simply a home whose logic is legible.
body_html:
California's insurer of last resort is no longer a story confined to the canyons. New reporting in the Los Angeles Times shows that the FAIR Plan, the state's residual market for homes that cannot find coverage elsewhere, is increasingly absorbing properties that its own risk model classifies as low-risk. The paper's framing is direct: California's property insurance deserts are spreading into areas with low wildfire exposure.

The finding matters because it comes from inside the system. These are not assessments from critics of the FAIR Plan or from consumer advocates. They are the plan's own classifications of the homes it has taken on.

Source: Los Angeles Times, "California's property insurance deserts are spreading to low-risk fire areas," September 20, 2026.

What the FAIR Plan's Own Data Shows

396ZIP codes analyzed
9 in 10new policies rated low-risk
Mar 2025 – Jun 2026policy window

According to the Times, in 396 ZIP codes, nine out of ten policies added to the FAIR Plan between March 2025 and the end of June 2026 were deemed by the plan itself to be low-risk. The window opens in the weeks after the January 2025 Los Angeles fires and runs roughly sixteen months, the period in which non-renewals and the residual market moved to the center of California's housing conversation.

Read plainly, the data describes a mismatch. A residual market exists to hold risks that the voluntary market declines to write. When the overwhelming majority of new entrants in hundreds of ZIP codes are, by the plan's own measure, not high-hazard properties, the explanation for their arrival is unlikely to be hazard alone. Our reading is that availability of voluntary coverage, not the physical risk of the individual address, is now the binding constraint in a widening share of the state.

That distinction is important for anyone budgeting a home. Hazard is a property of land and climate. Availability is a property of carrier appetite, capital, and regulation, and it can shift faster than any fire map.

What It Means for Los Angeles Buyers

For years, the working assumption on the Westside was that location settled the insurance question. A flat lot in Beverly Hills read differently from a ridgeline in Malibu or a canyon in Topanga. The figures reported by the Times suggest that this shorthand is losing its reliability. A low-risk address is still an advantage, but it no longer guarantees a place in the voluntary market on its own.

For a buyer commissioning a new home, the practical consequence is a shift in where the insurability conversation begins. If the ZIP code carries less explanatory weight, the building itself has to carry more. What can be documented about the roof assembly, the eaves, the vents, the first five feet around the walls, and the envelope becomes the evidence a household brings to the table.

If the address no longer settles the coverage question, the architecture has to.

These are not only technical line items. They are architectural decisions with consequences for proportion and character: the depth and finish of an eave, the profile of a parapet, the material of a terrace edge, the way planting meets a wall. Resolved early, at the schematic stage, they become part of the composition. Resolved late, they read as additions. The Times data argues for moving them to the front of the design process, even on lots that have never been considered high-hazard.

Looking Ahead

The next FAIR Plan data releases will show whether the low-risk share keeps widening or stabilizes as the voluntary market rebuilds capacity. Either way, the lesson from these 396 ZIP codes holds: insurability in California is becoming a characteristic of buildings as much as of places. The homes best positioned for the next cycle will be the ones whose resilience is legible in their drawings, not argued after the fact.
